title: Rumi of Konya
hookLine: Jalal al-Din Rumi, scholar of Konya, whose life turns when he meets Shams of Tabriz

lines: A SCHOLAR, A PREACHER, A TEACHER.
cards: His name turns up on mugs, posters and wedding invitations. But the man behind the quotes wasn't a greeting-card poet.
He was a Muslim scholar, a preacher and a teacher of the law, in a city in the middle of what's now Turkey. He led prayers. He taught students.
He was respected and settled. Then a wandering stranger walked into his life, and the scholar's life turned.

teach.b: Jalal al-Din Muhammad was born, by the usual account, in 1207, around Balkh, in the eastern Persian-speaking world.
When he was a boy, his family moved west, just ahead of the Mongol invasions, and settled in Konya, in Anatolia.
That region was called Rum, after the old Roman lands, and that's his name: Rumi, the one from Rum. Muslims often call him Mawlana, our master.
His father was a preacher and scholar, and when his father died, Rumi took over his teaching.

Then, in 1244, a wandering dervish named Shams, from Tabriz, arrived in Konya. The stories of their first meeting are many, and they're later legends; nobody knows exactly what happened. What's certain is what followed.
The two became inseparable, talking for days on end. Rumi's students grew jealous. Shams left, came back, and a few years later disappeared for good.
Some said he was killed; the sources are unsure. Rumi searched for him and didn't find him.
And out of that grief, the scholar became a poet. He composed thousands of verses of love poetry, and named the collection after Shams.
Later he dictated his great work, the Masnavi, full of stories and verses of the Qur'an. The Rumi on the mug is often stripped of all that.
The early accounts describe a man who kept the prayers and the fasts, and his Masnavi draws on the Qur'an again and again. It all turned on one friend.

how: Muslims across Turkey, Iran, Central and South Asia read Rumi's Masnavi as a work of Islamic spirituality, and every December many gather in Konya to mark the night of his death, which his followers call his wedding night with God.

games.q: you're a respected scholar, and your closest friend has vanished. your students are relieved. what do you do?
o: go back to teaching law as before.
search for him, and pour the grief into poetry.
games.why: Rumi searched and didn't find him, and out of that grief came thousands of verses, named for Shams.

practice: Bring to mind one person who turned your life in a new direction: a teacher, a friend, a stranger for one afternoon who asked the question nobody else asked. Picture their face, and remember what you were like before, and after.
Living or gone, hold them a moment with thanks, and if you pray, pray for them by name.

wordCard.voice: Mawlana. Our master — the title given to Rumi of Konya, the scholar whose meeting with Shams of Tabriz turned him into a poet. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic, used in Persian and Turkish: our master, the title Rumi's followers gave him (Mevlana in Turkish).

carryVoice: Your line: the meeting. One friend, and a scholar became a poet. Day two hundred ninety-eight, done.
